question: Why do commercial planes fly at around 35,000 feet?

passages.title: Why 35,000 Feet Is The Sweet Spot For Commercial Flights
passages.text: Why 35,000 Feet Is The Sweet Spot For Commercial Flights Have you ever wondered why pilots always seem to announce that magical phrase — "Ladies and gentlemen, we've reached our cruising altitude of 35,000 feet" — not long after takeoff? As a passenger, this seemingly arbitrary number might not mean much. However, there's a very specific scientific reason behind why planes tend to cruise around this specific altitude — and it's all to do with aerodynamics. For commercial airlines, for example, choosing the right cruising altitude is a complex calculation that takes into account multiple priorities. From ensuring fuel efficiency to analyzing current weather patterns, the direction of travel, and even air traffic control requirements, airlines must adhere to the delicate balance of both keeping passengers safe and comfortable and ensuring the operation runs as smoothly as possible. So, what exactly makes 35,000 feet so special? Well, it turns out that this particular height generally offers the ideal combination of thinner air for better fuel efficiency and less turbulence (which is generally less of a big deal than it feels like, thankfully), while still maintaining enough density for optimal engine performance. NASHUA, N.H. — Look at the flight map on the seatback screen and there's a good chance the altitude will settle somewhere around 35,000 feet. Another flight might cruise at 33,000 feet or climb above 40,000, but commercial jets spend much of their time in a generally narrow band of the atmosphere. Flying high makes sense. The air gets thinner with altitude, which lessens aerodynamic drag and can help an aircraft cover more distance for the fuel it burns. If thinner air is better, though, why stop around 35,000 feet? The science behind this optimal altitude for planes The main reason that commercial planes prefer to fly at higher altitudes boils down to simple physics: As you climb higher into the atmosphere, the air gets thinner. This reduced air density means that there's less resistance against the aircraft — which allows it to fly faster and more efficiently, ultimately saving on time and fuel. This fundamental flying scenario, however, is also why it's so important for commercial aircrafts to maintain cabin pressure at all times — and why you need to put your oxygen mask on when a plane loses cabin pressure. At 35,000 feet, the air outside the plane is just too thin for humans to breathe normally, which means that if you're not properly protected, you could lose consciousness within seconds. Beyond safety concerns, and despite the benefits of flying in thinner air, there's also a pretty strict limit to how high planes can go. Often referred to as the "service ceiling," this crucial safety threshold typically hovers around 45,000 feet for commercial airlines. Anything beyond this point basically marks the danger zone where the air becomes too thin for an aircraft to generate enough lift to stay airborne. Other ways an aircraft's altitude plays a role in safety Beyond physics and fuel efficiency, flight paths and air traffic control also influence how an aircraft decides on its altitude selection in some pretty creative ways. For example, if there's a plane heading south, southwest, west, and northwest, it's typically required to cruise at even-numbered altitudes (think 36,000 feet). Meanwhile, planes flying in opposite directions stick to odd numbers (such as 35,000 feet). This organized system — with flights headed for different destinations separated by 1,000-foot increments — ultimately helps air traffic controllers maintain safe distances between all the aircraft currently sharing the airspace. The standard atmosphere at 35,000 feet is around minus 66°F (minus 54°C), and the speed of sound falls to about 660 mph (1,062 km/h), compared with 761 mph (1,225 km/h) at sea level. passages.text: If you glance at the flight map on the seatback screen, the number indicating the aircraft altitude is almost always the same: 35,000 feet (10,668 meters). No law demands it, and no airline manual treats it as sacred. But jet airliners flying from Seattle to Singapore keep settling into the same narrowband of sky, as if the atmosphere came with a built-in parking spot. The thin air that makes high-altitude flying cheaper also takes lift away from the wings and thrust away from the engines, while the safety margin narrows with every thousand feet. The result is a constant compromise between aerodynamics, engine performance, aircraft weight, winds, and air traffic control. And the altitude that makes the most sense at the beginning of a long flight may be completely different several hours later. Thin Air Makes High-Altitude Cruise More Fuel Efficient That compromise starts with something passengers rarely notice from the cabin: there is dramatically less atmosphere at 35,000 feet than there is at sea level. According to AirportFYI, the International Standard Atmosphere puts air at about 31% of its sea-level density at 35,000 feet, or roughly 0.024 pounds per cubic foot (0.38 kg per cubic meter). But even a progressively lighter jet eventually reaches a point where going higher brings a new problem: the two boundaries of safe high-altitude flight begin moving toward one another. Coffin Corner Limits How High Airliners Can Efficiently Cruise The higher an aircraft climbs, the less room it has between two very different aerodynamic problems. The first is flying too slowly and approaching a stall. The second is flying too quickly and encountering compressibility effects as the airflow over the wing approaches critical Mach. Because the speed of sound falls as temperature drops while the true airspeed required to generate lift rises in thinner air, the two boundaries eventually begin to converge. SKYbrary defines the coffin corner as the region where the stall boundary meets the critical Mach boundary, and notes that commercial aircraft generally avoid operating close to it.
